newsitem.title: GERMANY: Panel calls for massive German budget savings.
newsitem.headline: Panel calls for massive German budget savings.

text.p: Germany has fallen into a vicious circle of rising state spending, spiralling tax and welfare costs and a shrinking tax base which can be broken only by massive savings efforts, an independent advisory panel said on Friday.

"To break the vicious circle massive efforts to consolidate state budgets are necessary, in order to break rigid spending structures and dampen growth in spending," the so-called five "wise men" said in a report.
"That can only be achieved through a medium-term programme which is firmly implemented, regardless of the economic situation," the report added.
Describing German debt levels of over two trillion marks as "dramatic", the panel said that interest service costs had now reached 11.5 percent of state spending.

State spending has also hit a historic high at over half of gross domestic product, and Germany's pay-as-you-go pension and social security systems will force spending up in future as the country's average age rises.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition government has a goal of reducing state spending to 46 percent of GDP by the year 2000. The panel forecast state spending would fall next year to 49.5 percent of GDP from 50.5 percent in 1996.
"Consolidation policy should target not only avoiding future burdens, but also maintaining the ability of the economic system to function," the report continued.
Although savings would dampen state demand in the short term, in the longer term they would bring net benefits to the economy, it added.
In order to meet the criteria for European monetary union, savings should be spread between federal, state and local governments, the panel said.

It offered to draft an internal German "stability pact" to match a similar deal sought by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to enforce budget stability among European countries seeking to take part in the launch of a single currency.
The panel supported plans to cut taxes and simplify the German tax system, saying that a lightening of the overall tax burden of between 20 and 30 billion marks was needed.
